account: On 19 October 2023 the ocean advocacy group Oceana reported that, in its analysis of vessel tracking data from November 2020 to July 2022, 82% of boats ignored the voluntary 10-knot limit in Slow Zones. On 27 December 2023 the Gulf of Maine Winter Slocum glider acoustically detected North Atlantic right whales east of Portland, Maine. Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and NOAA's Northeast Fisheries Science Center operate the glider. Such gliders carry a DMON instrument running the Low-Frequency Detection and Classification System (LFDCS). The system matches pitch-tracked calls against a call library using quadratic discriminant function analysis. Shore-based analysts validate detections. On 29 December 2023 NOAA Fisheries announced a voluntary Right Whale Slow Zone bounded by 43°49'N, 43°09'N, 67°02'W and 68°57'W. It ran from 27 December 2023 through 11 January 2024. NOAA asked mariners to route around the area or transit at 10 knots or less. No source reports how vessels behaved inside this Slow Zone. On 20 January 2024 a glider made the first definite glider-based acoustic detection in southeast United States waters. In 2025 Indeck and colleagues, including the system's developer, reported that gliders had triggered or extended 51 of the 154 Slow Zones that acoustic detections triggered or extended in the program's first four years.

ai_role.statement: Automated classification produced the candidate detections. Analysts validated them on shore before NOAA acted. The resulting Slow Zone is voluntary.

fields.account: On 19 October 2023 the ocean advocacy group Oceana reported that, in its analysis of vessel tracking data from November 2020 to July 2022, 82% of boats ignored the voluntary 10-knot limit in Slow Zones. On 27 December 2023 the Gulf of Maine Winter Slocum glider acoustically detected North Atlantic right whales east of Portland, Maine. Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and NOAA's Northeast Fisheries Science Center operate the glider. Such gliders carry a DMON instrument running the Low-Frequency Detection and Classification System (LFDCS). The system matches pitch-tracked calls against a call library using quadratic discriminant function analysis. Shore-based analysts validate detections. On 29 December 2023 NOAA Fisheries announced a voluntary Right Whale Slow Zone bounded by 43°49'N, 43°09'N, 67°02'W and 68°57'W. It ran from 27 December 2023 through 11 January 2024. NOAA asked mariners to route around the area or transit at 10 knots or less. No source reports how vessels behaved inside this Slow Zone. On 20 January 2024 a glider made the first definite glider-based acoustic detection in southeast United States waters. In 2025 Indeck and colleagues, including the system's developer, reported that gliders had triggered or extended 51 of the 154 Slow Zones that acoustic detections triggered or extended in the program's first four years.

purpose: The Low-Frequency Detection and Classification System was built to detect and classify baleen whale calls in near real time for management use. Triggering a Slow Zone is the use that it was built for.

ratings.reason: NOAA requested a voluntary speed reduction for an endangered species over a defined area for about 15 days. No source shows that a strike was averted or that vessels complied.
